title: Medication Errors, Near Misses and Incidents Procedure
summary: How every medicines error, near miss and medicines-related concern is handled: what care workers do at the visit, how the office obtains clinical advice, how medicines incidents are graded, investigated with the contributory factors framework and reported, how staff involved are supported and reassessed, and how learning is shared. For all employees, with the review and investigation steps for managers.

keyPoints.intro: Medicines errors happen even in careful teams. What matters is that the person is made safe, the office gets clinical advice and every error and near miss is reported so we can stop it happening again.
points: Make the person safe first. Call 999 if they seem unwell after an error, may have taken more than the eMAR allows (an extra dose or someone else's medicine) or nobody knows what they took. Stay until the crew or a colleague take over.

Never try to put an error right yourself. Do not skip, delay, add or double a dose, give a missed dose late or make the person sick. Give nothing more of that medicine until the office passes on clinical advice.

Phone the office, or the On-call Manager out of hours, at once from the home when an error has reached the person, and before you leave for a near miss. If nobody answers within 15 minutes, phone the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager.
Stay with the person while the office gets advice, for up to 30 minutes after the planned end of the visit. Your time is paid and the office covers your next visits.

Keep the evidence. Leave packs, labels and the monitored dosage system as they are, seal any dose you took out but did not give, and never throw anything away, take medicines or packs from the home or alter a record.
Tell the person honestly what happened, say sorry and say a manager will be in touch. Do not guess at causes or blame anyone.
Record the correct outcome on the eMAR, the care you gave and the advice in the daily visit notes, and the incident in the incident log before the end of your shift.

Report near misses, errors you find from earlier visits, pharmacy, hospital and family errors, and your own mistakes. Honest mistakes are treated as a chance to learn; hiding an error or altering a record is a disciplinary matter.

Also phone before you leave about declined doses, side effects such as falls or drowsiness after a medicines change, stockpiling, missing medicines, or anyone withholding, taking or misusing the person's medicines.

After an error of yours reaches a person, or two recording errors in 3 months, you are reassessed before giving medicines alone again, within 5 working days of the decision or of any retraining. You are paid for visits taken off your rota.
If you are asked for a written account, give it within 3 working days in paid time. Your Field Care Supervisor will talk through what happened and the support you need.

blocks.p: {{organisation}} reports, reviews and learns from every medicines error, near miss and medicines-related concern, however small. A care worker is usually alone with the person when something goes wrong, so this procedure sets out what they do at the visit, how the office obtains clinical advice and who decides what happens next.

We investigate why an error happened, not who to blame. Staff who report honestly are supported; deliberate harm, recklessness and dishonesty are not tolerated. People and their families are told openly what happened and what we changed. It helps us meet regulations 12(2)(g), 13, 17 and 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 and NICE guideline NG67 on reporting and learning from medicines-related problems. Timescales are our policy unless stated as law.

This procedure makes sure the person is made safe and clinical advice obtained before any further dose, every medicines incident is reviewed the same day, investigated and reported, staff are treated fairly, and learning is shared.

This procedure applies to all employees, including bank and agency workers, and to every medicines-related problem involving a person we support, including errors by others that we find and concerns about medicines the person or family manage.

The Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy owns the incident log, severity scale, investigation levels and closure; this procedure adds what is specific to medicines. Controlled drug discrepancy checks, eMAR corrections, declined doses and missed visits are owned by the Controlled Drugs in the Community Procedure, the Medicines Administration Records (MAR and eMAR) Procedure, the Consent, Mental Capacity and Declined Medicines Policy and the Missed, Late and Short Visits Procedure.

rows: Medication error
Any preventable mistake in prescribing, dispensing, supplying, storing, giving, recording or monitoring a medicine, whether or not it causes harm, including a medicine we order running out.
Near miss
An error noticed before it reached the person, such as an eMAR set-up error found at the second check.
Reached the person
A dose was taken, applied, missed or given at the wrong time because of the error, whether or not harm followed.
Medicines incident
Any medication error, near miss or other medicines-related problem entered in the incident log.
Clinical advice
Advice about the person and the next dose from the prescriber, a pharmacist, NHS 111 or the 999 service, recorded with the adviser's name, role, organisation and the time.
High-risk medicine

For this procedure: opioids and other controlled drugs, insulin and other diabetes medicines, anticoagulants (blood thinners), medicines for epilepsy, sedatives and sleeping tablets, methotrexate, lithium and digoxin.

blocks.p: The Directors scrutinise quarterly medicines incident trends. The Nominated Individual agrees the terms of reference for, approves and closes every Comprehensive medicines investigation.

The Registered Manager, as medicines lead, owns this procedure and leads Comprehensive investigations and the quarterly trend review. The Registered Manager or Deputy Manager makes the same-day review, grading, reporting and worker decisions; the Deputy Manager leads Enhanced investigations and the monthly check.

subsections.heading: Care Coordinators, Field Care Supervisors, Office staff and On-call Manager

blocks.p: Office staff, and the On-call Manager out of hours, take the call, obtain clinical advice and escalate; the On-call Manager never closes a medicines incident or decides that an external report is not needed. Care Coordinators follow up advice, tell partners, update the care plan and eMAR and brief the care team. Field Care Supervisors carry out in-home checks after errors, reassessments and supervision discussions. Both carry out Standard investigations once trained.

Care workers follow 'Immediate action at the visit', give accurate accounts and apply the changes they are briefed on. The HR Manager records interim measures and reassessments and books training needs within 5 working days.

Care workers report everything below by phone to the office, or the On-call Manager out of hours, speaking to a person. Rows 1 to 5 and 7 always go in the incident log; row 6 does when the person came to harm or the owning document says so.

rows: 1. An error that reached the person
Wrong medicine or dose, extra or missed dose, dose too early or late, wrong person, dose given against a refusal
At once, from the home
2. A near miss
Wrong pack picked up and spotted; dose prepared for the wrong time and not given
Before you leave
3. An error from an earlier visit or by someone else
Monitored dosage system compartment wrong or already empty, old patch not removed, label not matching the eMAR, discharge medicines missing
At once if a dose is affected, otherwise before you leave
4. A recording problem
Dose given but not recorded, wrong outcome recorded
Before you leave
5. A stock or supply problem
Controlled drug count wrong, medicines missing, run out, damaged or out of date, fridge outside 2 to 8 degrees
At once for a counted controlled drug, otherwise before you leave
6. A concern about the person
Declined doses, medicines not taken as prescribed, possible side effects such as falls or drowsiness after a medicines change, changes in health or capacity, stockpiling
Before you leave; 999 for danger signs, including sudden confusion
7. A concern about someone else
Someone withholding, taking or misusing the person's medicines or hiding medicine in their food; pressure on you to hand medicines over
Before you leave, from outside if the person who may be responsible is present or you feel unsafe

blocks.p: If nobody answers within 15 minutes, the care worker phones the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager directly. An informed decision to decline, a when required medicine not needed and a dose left out under an approved arrangement are not errors; the documents that own them apply.

steps: Check the person. Call 999 if they show any sign of being unwell after an error (difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, collapse, very hard to wake, slow or shallow breathing, a seizure, chest pain or new confusion), may have taken more of any medicine than the eMAR or pack allows (an extra or double dose, a dose over a limit, or a medicine prescribed for someone else), or nobody knows what or how much they took. This is a possible overdose under the First Aid Procedure. Stay, still checked in and paid, until the crew arrive or a colleague takes over, while the office covers your next visits; tell the call handler what was taken, when and how much, and show the crew the eMAR and packs.

Stop. Give nothing more of the medicines involved and never try to put the error right by skipping, delaying, adding or doubling a dose, giving a missed dose late or making the person sick. Give other medicines due as normal unless the error leaves you unsure; then ask the office first.
Phone the office or On-call Manager at once where the error reached the person, otherwise before you leave, with the medicines, what happened, when, how much and how the person is now.

Stay with the person while the office obtains clinical advice, for up to 30 minutes after the planned end of the visit, and follow the advice it passes on. If advice will come later, the office arranges another visit or call to act on it and reallocates your next visits. Your time is paid.

Keep the evidence: leave packs, labels, the monitored dosage system and any patch where they are, and seal and label any dose taken out but not given, keeping it with the person's medicines. Never take medicines or packs away from the home.
Tell the person, and any family member present with the person's agreement, simply what happened, say sorry and say that a manager will be in touch, without guessing at causes or blaming anyone.

Record the correct outcome on the eMAR at the time, never Given for a dose you did not see taken, and ask the office to correct any earlier record. In the daily visit notes, record the care you gave, the person's condition, the advice and that an incident was reported. Enter the incident log before the end of your shift; if you cannot use CareFlow, the office records your account during the call.

Office staff (the On-call Manager out of hours) record the call and all advice in the daily visit notes as it happens. In office hours they pass the report at once to the Care Coordinator and the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager.

For every error that reached the person, every dose affected by a near miss and every error found from an earlier visit, the office obtains clinical advice before the next dose of the medicines involved: in office hours from the supplying pharmacist or GP practice; out of hours, or where neither can advise within 30 minutes of the call, from NHS 111. The advice is read back. If the person deteriorates, the office tells the care worker to call 999.

The Registered Manager or Deputy Manager (On-call Manager out of hours) decides within 1 hour of the call what keeps the person safe until the next visit, such as who watches for which signs and for how long, an extra visit or welfare call, or the worker stopped from medicines visits, and records it in the incident log entry. They also check the care worker is fit to go on to their next visit.
The Care Coordinator (On-call Manager out of hours) briefs the next care worker by phone before their visit and records the briefing in the daily visit notes.

The Registered Manager or Deputy Manager reviews the incident the same day, and at once for a Critical incident or possible serious injury, by phone with the On-call Manager when it is reported out of hours, and records the grade, investigation level and each external reporting decision with reasons.

Within 2 working days of any error that reached the person, or any unexplained discrepancy, a Field Care Supervisor or authorised Senior Care Worker checks all the person's medicines in the home against the eMAR for related errors.
The Care Coordinator reviews the person's medicines support within 7 days, and before the next visit where the method is no longer safe.

blocks.p: Errors by others: the office tells the pharmacy the same day of a dispensing or labelling error and gets a corrected supply before the next dose; the Care Coordinator tells the prescriber the same day of a suspected prescribing error, and any other provider involved the same working day. Hospital discharge errors follow the Medicines Changes, Transfers of Care and Hospital Discharge Procedure. Where a relative or anyone else gave more than the eMAR or pack allows, the same 999 rule applies and the Registered Manager considers safeguarding. Where a family member or informal carer giving medicines under the care plan made the error, the Care Coordinator discusses it with them within 2 working days and reviews who does what in the care plan.
Medicines incidents are graded on the scale in the Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy. Timescales run from the report, and the investigation lead was not involved in the events.

rows: Low
Near miss; recording error that did not affect any dose; storage problem found before any dose was affected
Standard, within 5 working days
Medium

Any error that reached the person without lasting harm; a time-sensitive dose outside its window or missed; advice or treatment from a GP, NHS 111, pharmacist, nurse, ambulance crew or emergency department without admission
Enhanced, within 10 working days
High

Hospital admission, or harm lasting or likely to last 28 days or more; a dose given against a refusal or covertly without an approved plan; possible neglect or abuse by our staff; any matter reported to the police
Comprehensive: terms of reference within 2 working days, report within 10 working days
Critical
Death or permanent harm the error caused or may have contributed to; serious harm to more than one person from one cause, such as a wrongly filled pharmacy batch
Comprehensive, as for High

blocks.p: Where the outcome is uncertain, the higher grade applies until it is known. At least Enhanced: any Low incident that could credibly have caused serious harm (such as a near miss with a high-risk medicine), an incident meeting a pattern trigger in 'Medicines incidents and safeguarding', and any incident where a worker's practice is in question. An incident decided notifiable under the duty of candour moves to Comprehensive on the day of that decision.

subsections.heading: How a medicines incident is investigated

steps: Gather the eMAR and its audit trail, labels and packs, the medicines section of the care plan, visit check-in and check-out times, the rota with travel time and visit length, training and competency records, and earlier incidents for the person and the worker.

Obtain accounts from the staff involved within 3 working days, in paid time, and offer the person and their family a conversation within 5 working days of an Enhanced or Comprehensive investigation starting.
Ask the supplying pharmacist or the GP practice for their view where dispensing, labelling or the clinical effect is in question.

Record in the investigation in the incident log entry, following the Skills for Care summary and action planning form, how each relevant factor in the five domains below contributed. Human error or a procedure not followed is never the final finding.

Agree actions, each with an owner, a due date and the finding it addresses. Actions protecting the person are done before their next visit; practice-changing actions go into the service improvement plan within 5 working days of completion.

rows: 1. Situational factors
The worker (fatigue, rushing, distraction, inexperience); the task (unfamiliar formulation, unclear care plan); the person (asleep, declining, complex needs); the team
2. Working conditions
Rota pressure, travel time, overrunning or short visits, sickness cover; support out of hours; unavailable medicines, monitored dosage systems, measuring equipment
3. Organisational factors

The person's home (lighting, where medicines are kept, who else has access); other services (GP practice, pharmacy, hospital, community nurses, family); short-notice starts and discharges; training and competency
4. Latent and external factors
Packaging, look-alike names, people with similar names, ambiguous directions; our policies, commissioner guidance, the care plan and eMAR set-up
5. Communication and culture
Whether procedures were usually followed, fear of reporting, earlier near misses or audit findings not acted on; communication between office, care workers, family and professionals

sections.heading: Supporting and managing the staff involved

blocks.p: Before any action concerning a worker, the Registered Manager records the four fair culture questions in the Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy. Where a worker's practice put a person at risk, the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager (On-call Manager out of hours, confirmed by 10am the next working day) decides the same day on the least restrictive measure: working alongside a competent colleague, stopping one medicine or formulation, or removal from medicines visits. The Care Coordinator (On-call Manager out of hours) changes the rota the same day so no visit is missed or late. The worker is told why in person and in writing within 1 working day and paid for visits taken off their rota; the measure is reviewed at least every 5 working days. An agency worker does no medicines visits for us until our Field Care Supervisor has reassessed them, and the Registered Manager tells their agency the same working day.

blocks.p: After a distressing medicines incident the Field Care Supervisor contacts the worker within 1 working day and offers a debrief within 3 working days; the employee assistance programme is also available. A worker distressed during their run may stop for the day, with visits covered and rostered hours paid. While an investigation is open, supervision covers wellbeing and support, never the facts under investigation.

Under regulation 13, deliberately withholding a medicine, using one to sedate or control a person, giving one against a refusal or covertly without an approved plan, and theft, misuse or unexplained loss of a person's medicines are always referred to the local authority under the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure.

The safeguarding lead (On-call Manager out of hours) also decides, within 1 hour of the report, whether any medicines incident that caused harm, or a pattern, may be neglect. A pattern is two medicines incidents of the same type for one person in 4 weeks, three incidents of any type for one person in 90 days, or two controlled drug discrepancies for one person in 4 weeks. Referral is made the same working day, or at once if the person is at immediate risk.
Where staff may be responsible, the Managing Allegations Against Staff Procedure also applies and the Nominated Individual is told within 24 hours. Care workers never challenge or search anyone.

Each decision below, including a decision that a report is not needed, is recorded with its reason in the incident log entry at the initial review. RIDDOR reports follow the RIDDOR Reporting Procedure, DBS and professional regulator referrals the Staff Fitness Concerns and DBS Referrals Procedure, and LeDeR and insurer reports the Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy.

sections.heading: Side effects and the Yellow Card scheme

blocks.p: A suspected side effect of a correctly given medicine is not a medication error but is always reported. The office obtains advice straight away where it may be needed before the next dose; otherwise the Care Coordinator contacts the GP or pharmacist the same day. A side effect needing treatment beyond first aid also goes in the incident log.

Anyone can report a suspected side effect to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme, and the Care Coordinator offers the person and their named contact help to do so. Where the person asks us to report, or the side effect needed 999 or hospital treatment, the Care Coordinator tells the prescriber and submits a Yellow Card report within 2 working days with the person's consent, or under a best interests decision where they lack capacity, recording the reference in the incident log entry or care plan.

A medicine that seems faulty, of poor quality or fake is not used: it is sealed and kept with the person's medicines, the pharmacy is told the same day and the Registered Manager reports it through Yellow Card within 2 working days.

The written information on medicines concerns, complaints and advocacy given when medicines support starts also covers the Yellow Card scheme. The Care Coordinator gives it again after any medicines incident that reached the person and at each annual care plan review, with the date and format recorded in the care plan.

A medicines concern from the person, family or a professional is entered in the incident log the same working day by whoever receives it. Where the person wants to complain, the Complaints Policy and Procedure also applies; a complaint alleging abuse goes through the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure first. Where a person has substantial difficulty taking part in an investigation or candour conversation and nobody suitable can support them, the Care Coordinator asks the local authority in writing within 2 working days to consider an independent advocate.

bullets: Monthly: the Deputy Manager reports every medicines incident by type, stage, grade and branch, with near misses alongside errors, in the quality dashboard by the 7th working day.

Quarterly: the Registered Manager's trend review (stage, type, medicine group, time of day, care run, contributory factor domain, repeated incidents for one person or worker) goes in the quarterly medicines governance report. The same error type affecting 3 or more people in a branch in a month, or a 50% rise on the previous 3-month average, goes to the Nominated Individual within 2 working days, with a thematic review within 1 month.

Staff and partners: learning is shared as the Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy sets out, with a medicines item at every quarterly staff team meeting and in the six-monthly You said, we did summary. Repeated partner issues go to the commissioner.
Audit: recurring error types become a focus of the next monthly eMAR audit and observed medicines practice spot checks.

blocks.p: The incident log entry holds the report, grade, clinical advice, decisions with reasons, investigation with its contributory factors, actions, notifications and candour record, under one reference used in every related record. Dose outcomes and corrections are on the eMAR; care given, calls, advice and briefings in the daily visit notes; safeguarding concerns in the safeguarding records; interim measures and reassessments in the staff record and the training and compliance records. Retention follows the Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy.

blocks.p: Reassessment after an error follows the Medicines Training and Competency Assessment Procedure. Each investigator's first two medicines investigations are checked by the Registered Manager before closure. Staff acknowledge this procedure in CareFlow by the deadline in the Induction and Care Certificate Procedure and within 14 days of each new major version; a minor version needs no new acknowledgement.

blocks.p: Targets: 100% of errors reaching the person with clinical advice recorded before the next dose; 100% reviewed the same day; 100% of reassessments completed before further unsupervised medicines support; at least 95% of investigations on time. Every shortfall becomes an action in the service improvement plan with an owner and a deadline.

This procedure is reviewed every 12 months by the Registered Manager and approved by the Directors under the Policy Management and Document Control Policy, and sooner after a change in law or national guidance, a serious medicines incident, an inspection finding, or when monitoring shows our arrangements are not working.
